title: Nervous System
tagline: The neuron, brain and spinal cord, reflex action and the reflex arc, and the division of nervous control.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: The nervous system is the body's fast electrochemical control network. Structural and functional units called neurons carry impulses from receptor to effector; the brain integrates, the spinal cord relays and protects, and nerves link them to every part of the body. This chapter covers the three kinds of neurons and the myelinated nerve fibre, the divisions of the nervous system (central, peripheral, sympathetic and parasympathetic), the regions of the brain and their functions, and the reflex arc — the automatic pathway behind reflexes, with the spinal cord serving as the integrating centre so the brain learns of the event only afterwards.

facts.label: Impulse speed
facts.value: Up to ~100 m/s along myelinated nerve fibres

facts.label: Reflex arc
facts.value: Receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → effector

learn.title: The neuron and nerve impulse conduction

blocks.text: A neuron consists of a cell body with nucleus and Nissl granules, a single long axon carrying impulses away from the cell body, and branching dendrites that receive impulses from other neurons. Sensory (afferent) neurons carry impulses from receptors toward the central nervous system; motor (efferent) neurons carry impulses from the CNS to effectors such as muscles and glands; association (relay) neurons connect them within the CNS. Many axons bound together form a nerve. Along the axon the impulse travels as a wave of depolarisation — sodium ions rush in, reversing the membrane potential, and the wave propagates. Myelin sheath, formed by Schwann cells, insulates the fibre and forces the impulse to jump between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), which greatly increases speed. At the synapse, the impulse triggers release of a chemical neurotransmitter that diffuses across the cleft and depolarises the next neuron; the one-way, all-or-nothing behaviour of synapses ensures impulses travel in a single direction and prevents backflow.

items.meaning: Structural and functional unit of the nervous system; cell body, axon and dendrites.
Single long fibre carrying impulses away from the cell body.
Branching extension receiving impulses from other neurons.
Fatty insulating layer by Schwann cells; speeds conduction by saltatory leaps.
Junction between two neurons where a neurotransmitter crosses the cleft.
Ribosome-rich bodies in the cell body, abundant in active neurons.

items: Sensory neuron: long dendron from receptor to cell body in dorsal root ganglion; carries to CNS.
Motor neuron: cell body in ventral horn; long axon to effector; carries from CNS.
Association neuron: entirely within CNS; links sensory and motor pathways.
Impulse = wave of depolarisation propagating along the axon membrane.
Myelin + nodes of Ranvier -> saltatory conduction -> much faster speed.
Synapse: neurotransmitter ensures one-way transmission and prevents re-excitation backflow.
Nerve = bundle of axons wrapped in connective tissue; a tract is a bundle within the CNS.

items.text: Pulling your hand from a hot stove happens before you feel the pain — the reflex arc completes via the spinal cord first.
items.note: The brain receives the pain message afterwards, along the same sensory neuron.

items.text: Multiple sclerosis damages myelin, slowing conduction and disrupting coordination.
items.note: Shows the myelin sheath's role in fast, reliable transmission.

learn.title: Brain, spinal cord and nervous divisions

blocks.text: The brain lies protected within the cranium, wrapped in three meninges and floated in cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions it against shock. The cerebrum is the largest part, its folded cortex carrying centres for intelligence, memory, reasoning, speech and voluntary movement, with the left hemisphere controlling the right side of the body and vice versa. The cerebellum coordinates muscular activity, posture and balance; damage causes staggering, uncoordinated movement. The medulla oblongata controls involuntary vital activities — heartbeat, breathing, swallowing, vomiting — and connects the brain to the spinal cord. The hindbrain also includes the pons, which assists breathing regulation. The spinal cord runs down the vertebral canal: it conducts impulses to and from the brain and is the integrating centre of reflex actions. The peripheral nervous system comprises cranial and spinal nerves; of these, the autonomic nervous system has two opposed branches — the sympathetic division increases heart rate, dilates airways and prepares the body for action, while the parasympathetic division slows the heart, promotes digestion and conserves energy.

items: Cerebrum: intelligence, memory, thought, speech, voluntary action; opposite-side control of the body.
Cerebellum: coordination, posture, balance; damage -> loss of muscular coordination.
Medulla oblongata: heartbeat, breathing, swallowing — involuntary vital centres.
Spinal cord: relay between brain and body; centre for reflex actions; protected by vertebrae.
Meninges + cerebrospinal fluid: protection from shock and infection.
Sympathetic: 'fight or flight' — faster heart, dilated bronchioles, pupil dilation, inhibited digestion.
Parasympathetic: 'rest and digest' — slows heart, stimulates digestion, conserves energy.

items.text: In an exam your heart beats faster and digestion pauses — sympathetic dominance under stress.
items.note: The two autonomic branches act antagonistically to fine-tune organ activity.

items.text: A blow to the back of the head can damage the cerebellum — balance and coordination suffer.
items.note: Brain injury location predicts the deficit — cortex, cerebellum or medulla.

items.meaning: Largest brain region; conscious thought, memory and voluntary movement.
Hindbrain region coordinating movement, posture and balance.
Region controlling involuntary vital activities such as heartbeat and breathing.
Autonomic branches preparing for action / conserving energy.

learn.title: Reflex action and the reflex arc

blocks.text: A reflex action is a fast, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus — withdrawing a hand from flame, blinking at dust, salivating at food. The pathway is the reflex arc: stimulus excites a receptor; a sensory neuron carries the impulse to the spinal cord; an association neuron relays it; a motor neuron carries the command to an effector, which responds; the brain receives the sensory information separately, which is why pain is felt a moment after the withdrawal. Because the integrating centre is in the spinal cord, no conscious delay occurs, protecting the body from harm. Reflexes may be unconditioned (inborn, e.g. knee-jerk, blinking) or conditioned (learned, e.g. salivating at the sight of food). The knee-jerk is a spinal reflex used clinically: an absent or exaggerated response indicates damage at a specific spinal level. Every reflex arc needs all five components — receptor, sensory neuron, relay neuron, motor neuron and effector — because breaking any link abolishes the response.

items: Reflex arc: receptor -> sensory neuron -> relay (association) neuron in spinal cord -> motor neuron -> effector.
Response is faster than a thought-through action because it bypasses the brain.
Unconditioned reflexes are inborn (blink, knee-jerk); conditioned reflexes are learned (salivation at a bell).
Sensory pathway enters the cord via dorsal roots; motor signals leave via ventral roots.
The brain learns of the reflex afterwards via ascending tracts — hence pain after withdrawal.
Damage anywhere in the arc abolishes the reflex — a clinical test of pathway integrity.

items.text: Knee-jerk: tap the patellar tendon -> stretch receptor fires -> sensory neuron -> lumbar cord -> quadriceps contracts, leg kicks.
items.note: Tests spinal levels L3–L4; used in routine neurological examination.

items.text: Blinking when dust approaches the eye protects the cornea before any conscious decision forms.
items.note: A protective reflex with the eye itself as receptor and eyelid muscles as effector.

keyPoints: Neuron = cell body + axon + dendrites; the structural and functional unit of the nervous system.
Sensory neurons carry to the CNS; motor neurons carry from it; relay neurons connect them.
Myelin sheath with nodes of Ranvier speeds conduction by saltatory conduction.
Synapses use neurotransmitters and ensure one-way transmission.
Cerebrum: thought, memory, voluntary action; cerebellum: coordination and balance; medulla: vital involuntary centres.
Spinal cord relays impulses and integrates reflexes.
Reflex arc: receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron → motor neuron → effector.
Reflexes are fast and involuntary because the brain is not in the immediate loop.
Sympathetic prepares for action; parasympathetic conserves energy — they act antagonistically.
experimentFocus: Reflex testing: knee-jerk (patellar, L3–L4), blink, withdrawal — know receptor, effector and cord level for each.
Distinguish conditioned from unconditioned reflexes by origin: inborn versus learned through association.
If a reflex is absent, locate the break: receptor, nerve, cord segment or effector — a clinical-reasoning style question.
examFocus: Reflex arc answers must name all five components in order — each missing part costs a mark.
Brain region questions pair function with region: cerebrum-cognition, cerebellum-coordination, medulla-vital signs.
Neuron structure: name the parts and state what each carries — dendrite toward, axon away.
Autonomic comparisons expect one opposed pair of effects (heart rate, digestion) for each branch.

vocabulary.meaning: Nerve cell; the functional unit of the nervous system.
Fast involuntary automatic response to a stimulus.
Fatty sheath insulating axons and speeding impulses.
Brain region coordinating movement and balance.
Brain stem controlling involuntary vital functions.

questions.prompt: Which part of the brain controls balance and muscular coordination?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates muscular activity, posture and balance; damage causes uncoordinated, staggering movement.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the cerebrum — it controls voluntary movement initiation, not coordination and balance.

questions.prompt: The order of components in a reflex arc is:
options: Effector → motor neuron → relay neuron → sensory neuron → receptor
Receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron → motor neuron → effector
Receptor → motor neuron → relay neuron → sensory neuron → effector
Sensory neuron → receptor → effector → motor neuron
questions.answer: Receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron → motor neuron → effector
questions.explanation: The stimulus excites a receptor; the sensory neuron carries the impulse to the cord, a relay neuron connects, the motor neuron carries the response command to the effector.
questions.commonMistake: Starting with the effector — effectors respond; receptors detect.

questions.prompt: Impulse conduction is fastest along a fibre that is:
questions.explanation: The myelin sheath insulates the axon so the impulse jumps node to node (saltatory conduction), greatly increasing speed.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing thin unmyelinated fibres — they conduct more slowly; myelin is the speed factor.

questions.prompt: Which division of the autonomic nervous system slows the heart and promotes digestion?
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic branch acts in 'rest and digest' conditions, slowing the heart and stimulating digestive activity.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing sympathetic — it does the opposite, preparing the body for exertion.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the fatty insulating layer around a nerve fibre is the ________ sheath, and the gaps between its cells are called ________ of Ranvier.
questions.explanation: Myelin sheath cells (Schwann cells) wrap the axon; the exposed gaps are the nodes of Ranvier where the impulse is regenerated.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the sheath with the axon membrane — myelin insulates, the membrane conducts.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: impulses cross a synapse by means of a chemical called a ________, which diffuses across the synaptic cleft and excites the next neuron.
questions.explanation: The neurotransmitter is released from the presynaptic terminal, crosses the cleft and depolarises the postsynaptic membrane.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the impulse jumps the gap electrically — the transmission is chemical, ensuring one-way flow.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a neuron and state the function of each part.
questions.answer: A neuron has three main parts. Dendrites are short branching extensions that receive impulses from other neurons and conduct them toward the cell body. The cell body contains the nucleus and numerous Nissl granules; it maintains the cell and integrates incoming signals. The axon is a single long fibre carrying impulses away from the cell body; it is often wrapped in a myelin sheath whose gaps (nodes of Ranvier) allow the impulse to jump and travel faster, and it branches at its end into terminals that connect to effectors or other neurons at synapses.
questions.explanation: Part → structure → function for all three regions; the myelin/nodes detail lifts the answer to full marks.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the direction of dendrites and axons — dendrites toward, axon away from the cell body.

questions.prompt: Explain why a reflex action is faster than a voluntary action.
questions.answer: In a reflex action the impulse passes from receptor through sensory, relay and motor neurons to the effector with the integrating centre in the spinal cord, so the shortest possible pathway is followed and no delay occurs while the brain processes the information. In a voluntary action the impulse must travel from receptor to the brain, where it is perceived, interpreted and a decision formed, before a command travels back down the spinal cord to the effector — a much longer pathway involving conscious processing. Additionally, the reflex pathway uses few synapses, each of which imposes a small delay, so minimising synapses also saves time; the brain receives news of the reflex only afterwards along ascending tracts.
questions.explanation: Both reasons matter: shorter pathway bypassing the brain, and fewer synapses; the delayed conscious perception explains why pain follows the withdrawal.
questions.commonMistake: Saying reflexes 'do not use nerves' — they use the full arc; it simply bypasses the brain.

questions.prompt: Describe the functions of the cerebrum, cerebellum and medulla oblongata, and explain how the brain is protected.
questions.answer: Cerebrum — the largest part of the brain, with a folded outer cortex containing centres for intelligence, memory, reasoning, speech and interpretation of sensory input; it initiates voluntary movements, and each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body. Cerebellum — coordinates muscular activity, maintains posture and equilibrium; damage results in uncoordinated, staggering movement. Medulla oblongata — part of the hindbrain controlling involuntary vital activities including heartbeat, breathing, swallowing and vomiting, and connecting the brain with the spinal cord. Protection: the brain is enclosed in the bony cranium; surrounded by three meningeal layers; and floated in cerebrospinal fluid within the ventricles and subarachnoid space, which cushions it against mechanical shock and helps prevent infection.
questions.explanation: Three regions with distinct functions plus three protective layers — the bony, membranous and fluid cushions.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting cerebrospinal fluid in the protection part — the cranium alone is only one of the three defences.

questions.prompt: A person touches a hot pan and withdraws the hand before feeling pain. Draw the reflex arc involved and explain why the pain is felt later.
questions.answer: Reflex arc: heat receptors in the skin of the finger are excited by the hot pan; the sensory neuron carries the impulse along its axon through the dorsal root into the spinal cord; in the cord a relay (association) neuron passes it directly to a motor neuron; the motor neuron carries the command along its axon to the flexor muscles of the arm, which contract and withdraw the hand. Meanwhile, other branches of the sensory pathway and ascending tracts carry the information up the spinal cord to the cerebrum, where it is interpreted as pain. Because this route to the cerebrum involves more synapses and a much longer distance than the short spinal circuit, the withdrawal is completed before the sensation of pain reaches consciousness.
questions.explanation: The arc must be drawn with all five components in order, then the delay explained by pathway length and synaptic count.
questions.commonMistake: Saying 'the brain is busy' — the correct reason is the longer, multi-synapse ascending pathway to the cortex.
